$$\min_{Z_1,\dots,Z_n}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\lVert x_i-\mu_{Z_i}\bigr\rVert_2^2$$

Finding structure without labels: k-means and hierarchical clustering

No one tells the algorithm what the groups are. k-means commits to \(k\) centres and pulls every point toward the nearest one; hierarchical clustering merges the closest groups, one pair at a time, and lets you choose the number of clusters afterwards.

Part A
The clustering problem
1

Learning without labels

Supervised learning is given pairs \((x_i, y_i)\) and learns to predict \(y\). Unsupervised learning is given only the \(x_i\), and must find patterns, structure or relationships in them on its own.

The workflow has the same two phases as supervised learning — fit, then predict — but what is fitted is a structure rather than a mapping to known answers.

Where it is used

  • Customer segmentation. Group users by browsing or purchase patterns so each segment can be treated differently.
  • Community detection. Group users of a network by shared interests or by who interacts with whom.
  • Also common: anomaly detection (points far from every cluster), image compression (replace each pixel colour with its cluster centre — "colour quantisation"), and dimensionality reduction such as PCA.
SupervisedUnsupervised (clustering)
Data\(\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}\)\(\{x_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\), no \(y\)
GoalPredict \(y\) for new \(x\)Discover groups of similar points
OutputA predictor \(f(x)\)Cluster labels \(Z_i\) (and, for k-means, centroids)
EvaluationCompare with the true labelsNo ground truth; use internal scores (SSE, silhouette) or domain judgement
The cluster numbers \(1,2,3\) returned by a clustering algorithm look like class labels. Why can't they be compared directly with class labels?

Cluster numbers are arbitrary names. Swapping "cluster 1" and "cluster 2" everywhere gives exactly the same grouping, so a clustering that finds the true groups perfectly could still get every "label" wrong. Comparisons with a ground truth have to be invariant to renaming — for example by checking which pairs of points are placed together.

2

Partitions and cluster assignments

A clustering of \(n\) points into \(k\) groups is just a label for each point. The difficulty is how many ways there are to choose those labels.

$$X=\{x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n\},\qquad x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$$

The task is to partition these \(n\) datapoints into \(k\) clusters. The partition is recorded with one cluster-assignment variable per point:

$$\{Z_1,Z_2,\dots,Z_n\},\qquad Z_i\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}$$

\(Z_i=j\) means "point \(x_i\) belongs to cluster \(j\)".

How many assignments are there?

Each point can take any of \(k\) labels, so there are \(k^n\) label vectors in total. Requiring every cluster to be non-empty removes some of them. By inclusion–exclusion, the number of label vectors that use all \(k\) labels is

$$N_{\text{onto}}(n,k)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^i\binom{k}{i}(k-i)^n \;=\; k!\,S(n,k)\;\le\;k^n$$

where \(S(n,k)\) is the Stirling number of the second kind: the number of ways to split \(n\) items into \(k\) non-empty unlabelled groups. The factor \(k!\) appears because every such split can be named in \(k!\) ways.

Small check: \(n=4\) points, \(k=2\) clusters

$$\sum_{i=0}^{2}(-1)^i\binom{2}{i}(2-i)^4 = 2^4-2\cdot1^4+0 = 14 = 2!\cdot S(4,2)=2\cdot 7$$

The 7 groupings are the 4 ways to put one point alone plus the 3 ways to split the points into two pairs.

Why is \(2^4-2=14\) the right count for \(n=4,\ k=2\), without using the general formula?

There are \(2^4=16\) ways to give each point label 1 or 2. Exactly two of them leave a cluster empty — "all 1" and "all 2" — so \(16-2=14\) use both labels.

3

Scoring a clustering

Among all those assignments, which one best describes the data? We need a number that is small when points sit close to the other members of their cluster.

The general notion is the spread within each cluster: how far the points of a cluster lie from that cluster's mean. Similar (close) points should share a cluster, so for a good assignment this spread should be low.

The k-means objective

$$F(Z_1,\dots,Z_n) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl\lVert {\color{#B23A6B}{x_i}} - {\color{#4A1E5C}{\mu_{Z_i}}} \bigr\rVert_2^{\color{#1F8A85}{2}}$$
Each pointEvery datapoint contributes once
Its own centroidThe mean of the cluster \(Z_i\) it is assigned to
Squared distanceSquared Euclidean length, so large deviations cost more

This quantity is also called the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS), inertia, or SSE. The centroid of cluster \(j\) is the mean of its members:

$$\mu_j=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\,\mathbb{1}\!\left(Z_i=j\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}\!\left(Z_i=j\right)}$$

The numerator adds up the points in cluster \(j\); the denominator counts them. \(\mathbb{1}(\cdot)\) is the indicator function: \(1\) when its argument is true and \(0\) otherwise.

Why the mean?

For a fixed set of points \(C_j\), the single centre \(c\) that minimises their total squared distance is exactly their mean. Setting the gradient to zero:

$$\nabla_c\sum_{x\in C_j}\lVert x-c\rVert^2=-2\sum_{x\in C_j}(x-c)=0\;\Longrightarrow\;c=\frac{1}{|C_j|}\sum_{x\in C_j}x=\mu_j$$

This is why "k-means" pairs squared Euclidean distance with averaging. Change the distance and the best centre changes too: with the sum of absolute distances \(\lVert x-c\rVert_1\), the best centre is the coordinate-wise median (k-medians).

Why the mean for squared distance, and the median for absolute distance

Both claims follow from the same question: if the centre \(c\) moves a little, does the total cost go up or down? Work in one dimension first, with points \(x_1,\dots,x_n\).

Squared distance: \(g(c)=\sum_i (x_i-c)^2\)
$$g'(c)=-2\sum_i (x_i-c)=2n\,(c-\bar x)$$

Each point pulls on \(c\) with a force proportional to its distance. The pulls balance where \(c=\bar x\), the mean. A point twice as far away pulls twice as hard, so one distant point can drag the centre a long way.

Absolute distance: \(h(c)=\sum_i |x_i-c|\)
$$h'(c)=\#\{x_i<c\}-\#\{x_i>c\}$$

Each point pulls with the same force, \(1\), whatever its distance. Moving \(c\) right makes every point on its left one step farther and every point on its right one step closer. The pulls balance when as many points lie on each side: at the median.

In two (or more) dimensions both costs split into one problem per coordinate, because \(\lVert x-c\rVert_2^2=\sum_j (x_j-c_j)^2\) and \(\lVert x-c\rVert_1=\sum_j|x_j-c_j|\). So the best centre is the coordinate-wise mean for squared distance and the coordinate-wise median for absolute distance.

The two cost surfaces in 3D

Below, the floor is the plane of candidate centres \(c=(c_1,c_2)\) and the height is the total cost of using \(c\) as the centre of five points (black dots). The lowest point of each surface is the best centre. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, and use the slider to move the fifth point away from the others.

  • The bowl is smooth. Squared cost is a quadratic in \(c\): \(\sum_i\lVert x_i-c\rVert^2=n\lVert c-\bar x\rVert^2+\sum_i\lVert x_i-\bar x\rVert^2\). Its level curves ("From above") are circles centred on the mean, and its floor height is exactly the within-cluster sum of squares.
  • The funnel is made of flat facets. Absolute cost is piecewise linear. It bends only along the lines \(c_1=x_{i1}\) and \(c_2=x_{i2}\) — the creases you can see — because that is where a point switches from one side of \(c\) to the other. Its level curves are polygons, and its lowest point sits where the median creases cross.
  • Why the outlier matters to one and not the other. Moving \(x_5\) farther right raises the left-hand bowl's wall on that side ever more steeply, tilting the whole bowl and moving its bottom. On the right, \(x_5\) is still just "one point to the right of \(c\)" with a pull of exactly \(1\), so the balance point does not move.
Two details

Even numbers of points. With an even count, any \(c\) between the two middle values balances the pulls, so the absolute-cost minimum is a flat edge or rectangle rather than a single point; by convention the median takes its midpoint.

Plain (unsquared) Euclidean distance \(\sum_i\lVert x_i-c\rVert_2\) gives a third answer, the geometric median. It is robust like the median but does not split by coordinate and has no closed form; it is found iteratively (Weiszfeld's algorithm).

Proof: the median minimises the sum of absolute distances

To mathematically prove that the median minimises the sum of absolute distances, we analyse the function's rate of change using piecewise differentiation. While it is true that the absolute value function \(f(x)=\lvert x\rvert\) is not differentiable exactly at \(x=0\), it is perfectly differentiable everywhere else, which provides the necessary mathematical framework to find the minimum.

Because the absolute distance (often called the Manhattan distance or \(L_1\) norm) is calculated independently for each axis, we can solve this for a single dimension. The logic then applies to every dimension, giving the coordinate-wise median.

The mathematical proof

Let \(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n\) be a set of 1-D data points. The cost function we want to minimise is the sum of absolute distances to a centre \(c\):

$$J(c)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\lvert x_i-c\bigr\rvert$$

To find the minimum, we take the derivative of \(J(c)\) with respect to \(c\). The derivative of a single absolute distance \(\lvert x_i-c\rvert\) depends on whether \(c\) is smaller or larger than the data point \(x_i\):

  • If \(c<x_i\), the distance decreases as \(c\) moves right, so the derivative is \(-1\).
  • If \(c>x_i\), the distance increases as \(c\) moves right, so the derivative is \(+1\).
  • If \(c=x_i\), the derivative is undefined: this is the sharp point (the kink) of the function.

Setting aside the exact points where \(c=x_i\) for a moment, the total derivative of the cost function is simply the sum of these \(+1\) and \(-1\) slopes:

$$\frac{d}{dc}J(c)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{sgn}\!\left(c-x_i\right)$$ $$\frac{d}{dc}J(c)=\#\{\,i: x_i<c\,\}\;-\;\#\{\,i: x_i>c\,\}$$

In words, the slope is (the number of points where \(c>x_i\)) minus (the number of points where \(c<x_i\)). For a function to reach its minimum, its derivative must be exactly \(0\), or cross from negative to positive. For the expression above to equal \(0\), the number of points smaller than \(c\) must be exactly equal to the number of points larger than \(c\).

The value that splits a dataset so that half the points lie on its left and half on its right is the definition of the median. \(\blacksquare\)

Odd and even numbers of points

The slope is an integer that only changes at the data points, so it is worth checking both cases. Sort the points as \(x_{(1)}\le x_{(2)}\le\dots\le x_{(n)}\).

Odd \(n=2m+1\). Just left of the middle point \(x_{(m+1)}\) the slope is \(m-(m+1)=-1\); just right of it, \((m+1)-m=+1\). The slope is never exactly \(0\): it jumps from negative to positive at \(x_{(m+1)}\), the kink. So the unique minimum is the median data point — the "cross from negative to positive" case above.

Even \(n=2m\). Strictly between \(x_{(m)}\) and \(x_{(m+1)}\) the slope is \(m-m=0\), so \(J\) is flat there and every \(c\in\bigl[x_{(m)},\,x_{(m+1)}\bigr]\) is a minimiser. The usual median, \(\tfrac12\bigl(x_{(m)}+x_{(m+1)}\bigr)\), is one of them.

Because \(J\) is convex — a sum of convex functions — the point where the slope changes from negative to positive is a global minimum, not just a local one. Formally, the condition is that \(0\) lies in the subdifferential \(\partial J(c)\), which handles the kinks directly.

An equivalent form

The within-cluster sum of squares can also be written purely through pairwise distances, which shows it really does measure how tightly the members sit together:

$$\sum_{x\in C_j}\lVert x-\mu_j\rVert^2=\frac{1}{2|C_j|}\sum_{x\in C_j}\sum_{x'\in C_j}\lVert x-x'\rVert^2$$
Cluster A holds the 1-D points \(\{0, 2, 4\}\). What is its contribution to \(F\)?

The mean is \(2\), so the contribution is \((0-2)^2+(2-2)^2+(4-2)^2=8\). Check with the pairwise form: the squared pairwise distances are \(4, 16, 4\), each counted twice in the double sum, giving \(48\); and \(48/(2\cdot 3)=8\).

4

Why brute force fails

The best clustering is the assignment that minimises \(F\). Finding it exactly is out of reach for all but tiny problems.

$$\min_{Z_1,Z_2,\dots,Z_n}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\lVert x_i-\mu_{Z_i}\bigr\rVert_2^2$$

Points are well clustered when they are close to the mean of their own cluster, so this is the quantity to minimise. Checking every assignment is hopeless because there are

$$k!\,S(n,k)\;\le\;k^n$$

of them. Even a modest \(n=100\) and \(k=3\) gives about \(3^{100}\approx5\times10^{47}\) assignments.

Worse, the problem is NP-hard: no known algorithm solves every instance in polynomial time. It remains NP-hard even for \(k=2\) when the dimension \(d\) is part of the input, and even in the plane (\(d=2\)) when \(k\) is part of the input.

Instead we use the k-means algorithm — more precisely Lloyd's algorithm — a heuristic that does not guarantee the optimum but finds a good assignment quickly.

Naming

"k-means" is used for two different things: the objective above (a problem) and Lloyd's algorithm (one heuristic for it). k-means++ (block 8) is a way to initialise Lloyd's algorithm, not a different objective.

Part B
k-means
5

Lloyd's algorithm

The objective has two sets of unknowns — the assignments \(Z\) and the centroids \(\mu\). Fixing one makes the other easy, so the algorithm alternates.

k-means (Lloyd's algorithm)
  1. Initialise the assignments \(\{Z_1^0,Z_2^0,\dots,Z_n^0\}\) (or, equivalently, \(k\) starting centroids). Set \(t=0\).
  2. Until convergence:
    1. Compute means. For \(j=1\) to \(k\): $$\mu_j^t=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\,\mathbb{1}\!\left(Z_i^t=j\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}\!\left(Z_i^t=j\right)}$$
    2. Reassign. For \(i=1\) to \(n\): $$Z_i^{t+1}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{j\in\{1,\dots,k\}}\;\bigl\lVert x_i-\mu_j^t\bigr\rVert_2^2$$
    3. \(t \leftarrow t+1\).
  3. Stop when no assignment changes, \(Z^{t+1}=Z^{t}\) (in practice also: centroids move less than a tolerance, or a maximum number of iterations is reached).

\(Z_i^t\) is the cluster of the \(i\)-th point after the \(t\)-th iteration.

A worked example in one dimension

Take \(x=\{1,2,4,10,11,12\}\), \(k=2\), and start with centroids \(\mu_1=1,\ \mu_2=2\).

StepCluster 1Cluster 2\(\mu_1\)\(\mu_2\)\(F\)
Assign to \((1,\,2)\)\(\{1\}\)\(\{2,4,10,11,12\}\)12249
Update means\(\{1\}\)\(\{2,4,10,11,12\}\)17.880.8
Reassign\(\{1,2,4\}\)\(\{10,11,12\}\)17.842.72
Update means\(\{1,2,4\}\)\(\{10,11,12\}\)2.33116.67
Reassignno point changes cluster → converged2.33116.67

In the second reassignment, point \(4\) is \(3\) from \(\mu_1=1\) but \(3.8\) from \(\mu_2=7.8\), so it switches; so does \(2\). Every row has an \(F\) no larger than the one above it — the subject of the next block.

What does one iteration of Lloyd's algorithm cost?

The reassignment step computes the distance from each of the \(n\) points to each of the \(k\) centroids in \(d\) dimensions: \(O(nkd)\). The update step touches each point once: \(O(nd)\). So one iteration is \(O(nkd)\), and a run of \(T\) iterations is \(O(nkdT)\) — linear in \(n\), which is why k-means scales to very large datasets.

During an iteration a cluster loses all its points. What happens, and what can be done?

Its mean is \(0/0\), undefined. Implementations handle this by re-seeding the empty centroid — commonly at the point that is currently farthest from its centroid (the one contributing most to \(F\)) — or by simply dropping the cluster. Good initialisation (block 8) makes this rare.

6

Convergence and local minima

Lloyd's algorithm always stops, and \(F\) never goes up on the way. But where it stops depends on where it started.

Why \(F\) never increases

Write the objective with both unknowns explicit, \(F(Z,\mu)=\sum_i\lVert x_i-\mu_{Z_i}\rVert^2\). Each half-step minimises \(F\) over one set of variables while holding the other fixed:

  • Reassign (fix \(\mu\), choose \(Z\)): each point picks the nearest centroid, so its own term can only shrink. \(F(Z^{t+1},\mu^t)\le F(Z^{t},\mu^t)\).
  • Update (fix \(Z\), choose \(\mu\)): by block 3, the mean is the best possible centre for each cluster. \(F(Z^{t+1},\mu^{t+1})\le F(Z^{t+1},\mu^t)\).
$$F^{0}\;\ge\;F^{1}\;\ge\;F^{2}\;\ge\;\cdots\;\ge\;0$$

This is coordinate descent. Since there are only finitely many assignments and \(F\) strictly decreases whenever the assignment changes (ties broken consistently), no assignment can repeat, so the algorithm terminates in a finite number of steps.

Stopping is not the same as winning

Termination guarantees a local minimum — no single reassignment or recentring helps — not the global one.

Watching Lloyd's algorithm run

The players below step through Lloyd's algorithm one half-step at a time, on 72 points in four groups. At each step, look for four things:

  • Which points switch cluster in a reassignment (they are ringed). When none switch, the algorithm stops.
  • How far each centroid moves in a mean update (dashed trail from its old position).
  • The objective \(F\) in the chart: it falls at every half-step and never rises (block 6).
  • The regions (Voronoi cells, block 7). Right after a mean update, a point lying in a region of a different colour is exactly a point that will switch at the next reassignment.

The algorithm here starts from \(k\) centroids rather than from assignments, so the loop begins with a reassignment; the highlighted line shows which step of the algorithm box is running. Use ← and → to step when the player has focus.

Run B is the situation of the right-hand panel in the static figure above, now seen forming. Two lessons follow. First, convergence is not a quality check: compare final values of \(F\) across runs, which is why libraries restart from several initialisations and keep the best. Second, the damage is done at the start: by the end of the first reassignment in B, one centroid already owns both upper groups, and no later step gives the starved region a centroid of its own. This is what k-means++ (block 8) is designed to prevent.

When a cluster goes empty

If the initial centroids are placed at arbitrary positions rather than at data points, a centroid can end up nearest to no point at all. Then step 2a asks for the mean of an empty set:

$$\mu_j^t=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\,\mathbb{1}\!\left(Z_i^t=j\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}\!\left(Z_i^t=j\right)}=\frac{0}{0}$$
Does an empty cluster mean \(k\) was wrong?

Usually not. The data in run C genuinely has four groups, and \(k=4\) is right; the empty cluster was caused by where centroid 4 started, not by the number of clusters. An empty cluster in the middle of a run is a symptom of a bad initialisation.

The common remedies, in order of preference: re-seed the empty centroid (at the point farthest from its centroid, as here, or by a k-means++ draw); restart from a new initialisation; or drop the cluster, which silently turns the run into one with \(k-1\) clusters and is rarely what you want.

An empty cluster does say something about \(k\) in two cases. If clusters keep going empty, or end with only one or two points, across many restarts with a good initialisation, the data probably does not support that many groups. And if \(k\) exceeds the number of distinct points, an empty cluster is unavoidable. Even then, choose \(k\) from the evidence in block 10 — the elbow, the silhouette, or a penalised objective — not from one run.

When can a cluster be empty?

If the starting centroids are \(k\) distinct data points — Option 1 of block 8, or k-means++ — no cluster can be empty after the first assignment: each centroid's own point is at distance \(0\) from it, so it is assigned there (barring exact ties). Empty clusters come from starting at arbitrary positions, as in run C, or from starting with random labels \(Z^0\) when \(n\) is small. They can also, more rarely, appear later in a run, when every point of a cluster moves to other centroids at the same reassignment.

In run B, every centroid is at the mean of its cluster and every point is at its nearest centroid. Why is that not enough to be the optimum?

Those two conditions only say that neither half-step can improve \(F\) on its own. Reaching the optimum from B would need a coordinated change — moving one of the two lower-left centroids all the way to the upper-right group — and that move first makes \(F\) much worse before it makes it better. Lloyd's algorithm never takes a step that increases \(F\), so it cannot get there.

Why re-seed the empty centroid at the point farthest from its own centroid, rather than at a random point?

The farthest point is the one contributing most to \(F\), so placing a centroid exactly on it gives the largest immediate drop in \(F\), and it usually lands in a region that is badly served — here, the upper-right group that had been merged with its neighbour. A random point is often in a group that already has a centroid, so the new cluster may empty again. The rule has a weakness: a single outlier is also "far", so with noisy data the re-seeded centroid can end up owning just that outlier.

Run A took 3 iterations and run B took 4. Does a run that takes longer end at a worse answer?

No. The number of iterations says how far the start was from some fixed point, not which fixed point it reached. Run C took 4 iterations and reached the same optimum as A. The quality of the result is judged by the final \(F\) (or by the silhouette and similar scores), never by how quickly the algorithm stopped. In general the iteration count varies with the data and the start; fewer than ten is typical in practice but not guaranteed.

Standard remedy: restarts

Run the algorithm several times from different initialisations and keep the run with the smallest \(F\). Library defaults do exactly this (for example scikit-learn's n_init). Better initialisation, the subject of block 8, reduces how many restarts are needed.

7

The geometry: linear boundaries and Voronoi regions

Once the centroids are fixed, the rule "go to the nearest centroid" slices space with straight lines.

Two clusters

With \(k=2\), a point \(x\) goes to cluster 1 when it is closer to \(\mu_1\) than to \(\mu_2\):

$$\lVert x-\mu_1\rVert_2^2\;\le\;\lVert x-\mu_2\rVert_2^2$$

Expand both sides with \(\lVert a-b\rVert^2=\lVert a\rVert^2-2a^{\top}b+\lVert b\rVert^2\):

$$\lVert x\rVert^2-2x^{\top}\mu_1+\lVert\mu_1\rVert^2\;\le\;\lVert x\rVert^2-2x^{\top}\mu_2+\lVert\mu_2\rVert^2$$

The \(\lVert x\rVert^2\) terms cancel — this is why the boundary is linear, not curved. Rearranging:

$$x^{\top}(\mu_2-\mu_1)\;\le\;\frac{\lVert\mu_2\rVert^2-\lVert\mu_1\rVert^2}{2} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad x^{\top}w\le b,\quad w=\mu_2-\mu_1,\;\; b=\frac{\lVert\mu_2\rVert^2-\lVert\mu_1\rVert^2}{2}$$

The boundary \(x^{\top}w=b\) is a linear decision boundary: a hyperplane perpendicular to \(\mu_2-\mu_1\). Because \(\left(\tfrac{\mu_1+\mu_2}{2}\right)^{\top}(\mu_2-\mu_1)=\tfrac{\lVert\mu_2\rVert^2-\lVert\mu_1\rVert^2}{2}=b\), it passes through the midpoint of the two centroids — it is their perpendicular bisector.

Any number of clusters

For \(k\) clusters, the region of cluster \(j\) is the set of points closer to \(\mu_j\) than to every other centroid. That is \(k-1\) conditions of the two-cluster kind, one per rival centroid:

$$R_j=\bigcap_{l\ne j}\left\{x:\;\lVert x-\mu_j\rVert\le\lVert x-\mu_l\rVert\right\}$$

Each region is therefore the intersection of \(k-1\) half-spaces bounded by perpendicular bisectors, which makes it a convex polytope. These regions are called Voronoi regions (or Voronoi cells), and together they form the Voronoi diagram of the centroids.

Because every region is convex, what kind of cluster can k-means never produce?

A non-convex one — a crescent, a ring, or a cluster wrapped around another. If two points belong to cluster \(j\), the whole segment between them lies in \(R_j\) as well. Block 11 shows what happens on data with such shapes.

How many boundaries can \(k\) centroids produce?

Every pair of centroids \(\mu_i,\mu_j\) has a perpendicular bisector, so there are \(\binom{k}{2}\) bisectors in all. Only some of them become Voronoi edges — pieces of boundary actually shared by two cells. A bisector is "used" when cells \(i\) and \(j\) touch along a segment, ray or line of positive length; if a third cell sits between them, or they meet at a single point only, it is not.

Write \(E\) for the number of Voronoi edges. (In \(d\) dimensions the shared boundaries are \((d-1)\)-dimensional faces rather than edges, and everything below holds with "edge" read as "shared face".)

$$k-1\;\le\;E\;\le\;\binom{k}{2}\qquad\text{for every } k\ge 2 \text{ distinct centroids, in any dimension}$$

Why \(E\le\binom{k}{2}\)

Each Voronoi edge separates exactly two cells \(i,j\), and lies on their bisector. Two cells can share at most one edge: both cells are convex (block 7), so their intersection is convex, and it lies inside one line — so it is a single segment, ray or line, a point, or empty. Different edges therefore belong to different pairs, and there are only \(\binom{k}{2}\) pairs.

Why \(E\ge k-1\)

Call two centroids adjacent when their cells share an edge. Walk in a straight line from \(\mu_i\) to \(\mu_j\), nudged slightly so it avoids the corners where three or more cells meet. Every time the walk leaves one cell it crosses an edge into an adjacent one, so the walk is a chain of adjacent cells from \(i\) to \(j\). Hence the adjacency graph — one node per centroid, one link per Voronoi edge — is connected, and a connected graph on \(k\) nodes has at least \(k-1\) links.

Both bounds are tight

  • Lower bound \(k-1\): put all centroids on one line. The cells are parallel strips, and only consecutive centroids touch: a chain of exactly \(k-1\) edges.
  • Upper bound \(\binom{k}{2}\): needs every pair of cells to touch. In the plane this is possible only for \(k\le 4\) (shown next); in three or more dimensions it is possible for every \(k\).
Arrangement of the \(k\) centroidsVoronoi edges \(E\)Role
All on one line\(k-1\)Absolute minimum
All on one circle\(k\)Minimum once not all on a line
\(k=4\): one centroid inside the triangle of the other three\(6=\binom{4}{2}\)Every bisector used

In three or more dimensions

The crossing-free argument is special to the plane. In three dimensions, links between centroids can pass over and under each other, and every pair of cells can share a face for any \(k\):

  • Corners of a tetrahedron (\(k=4\)): the four cells meet pairwise across all \(6\) faces.
  • Points on the twisted curve \((t,\,t^2,\,t^3)\): for any number of distinct values of \(t\), every pair of cells shares a face, so \(E=\binom{k}{2}\). The explorer below shows this for \(k=5\) to \(10\) — for instance \(45\) shared faces for \(k=10\), where the plane allows at most \(24\).
  • The case that matters for k-means: with \(d\ge k-1\) features, \(k\) centroids are almost always affinely independent (none lies in the flat spanned by the others). Then every pair of cells touches. To see why, the functions \(x\mapsto\lVert x-\mu_l\rVert^2-\lVert x-\mu_i\rVert^2\) for \(l\ne i\) are affine with linearly independent gradients \(2(\mu_i-\mu_l)\), so some \(x\) makes the one for \(l=j\) equal to \(0\) and all the others positive. That \(x\) is equally close to \(\mu_i\) and \(\mu_j\) and strictly farther from every other centroid: it lies on a face shared by cells \(i\) and \(j\).
SettingFewest edgesMost edgesIs \(\binom{k}{2}\) reachable?
Any dimension\(k-1\) (on a line)\(\binom{k}{2}\)Yes, for \(d\ge 3\) or \(k\le4\)
Plane, centroids not all on a line\(k\) (on a circle)\(3k-6\) (\(k\ge3\))Only for \(k=3,4\)
Plane, general position\(2k-3\)\(3k-6\)Only for \(k=3,4\)
\(d\ge k-1\), affinely independentexactly \(\binom{k}{2}\)Always
Why this matters for k-means

Pictures of k-means are almost always two-dimensional, where each cluster borders only a handful of others and most bisectors are unused. Real data usually has many more features than clusters. There, typically every pair of clusters shares a boundary, and each cluster's region is cut by all \(k-1\) of its bisecting hyperplanes. Intuitions such as "cluster 1 only competes with its neighbours" come from the plane and do not carry over.

Three centroids lie at \((0,0)\), \((2,0)\) and \((4,0)\). How many Voronoi edges are there, and which bisector is unused?

Two: the lines \(x=1\) and \(x=3\). The bisector of the outer pair is \(x=2\), but every point on it is closer to \((2,0)\), so it runs through the middle cell and separates nothing. This is the lower bound, \(E=k-1=2\).

Four centroids sit at the corners of a square. Why are there only 4 Voronoi edges, and what happens when one corner is pushed slightly inwards?

All four lie on one circle, so the four cells meet at a single point, the centre; the two diagonal pairs touch only at that point, which is not an edge. Pushing a corner inwards breaks the tie: two of the four cells now share a short segment near the centre, giving \(5=2k-3\) edges. Pushing it inside the triangle of the other three gives \(6=3k-6=\binom{4}{2}\).

Five centroids in the plane: can all \(\binom{5}{2}=10\) bisectors be Voronoi edges?

No. In the plane \(E\le 3k-6=9\), because the adjacency graph can be drawn without crossings and five points all joined to each other cannot be. The maximum, \(9\), is reached by a triangle with two centroids inside it. In 3D, five points on the twisted curve do reach \(10\).

8

Initialisation and k-means++

Since Lloyd's algorithm only finds a local minimum, its starting point matters. Two standard choices follow.

Option 1: random data points

  • Choose \(k\) points from the dataset uniformly at random to be the initial means.
  • Assign every point to its nearest mean, then continue running the algorithm as usual.

This is simple, but two starting means can easily land in the same true cluster, giving the kind of local minimum shown in block 6.

From k-means to k-means++: think "seeding"

Lloyd's algorithm does the hard work of finding the final cluster averages. The initialisation has a smaller, separate job: to give the algorithm a safe, sensible starting point. So the question changes from "where will the centres end up?" to "where is a good place to plant the seeds?" — and the answer k-means++ gives is: on the data points themselves, spread out across the data.

1. The problem with empty space

Suppose a starting centroid is dropped at a random position in the plane and lands in an empty region. It may end up nearest to no point at all. Its cluster is then empty, its mean is \(0/0\), and the run has to repair itself — exactly what happens in run C of the Lloyd's-algorithm player (block 6). If instead every seed is an actual data point, each seed is at distance \(0\) from at least one point (itself), so no cluster can be empty after the first assignment (as long as the seeds are distinct points). Every starting centroid sits in a populated neighbourhood.

2. A finite list of candidates

k-means++ wants the seeds to be spread out, and it does this by giving each candidate location a probability that grows with its squared distance to the nearest seed chosen so far:

$$P(x_i)=\frac{D(x_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}D(x_j)},\qquad D(x_i)=\min_{\text{seeds } s \text{ so far}}\;\lVert x_i-s\rVert^2$$

The denominator is a plain sum over \(n\) candidates, which is only possible because the candidates form a finite list. Choosing from every point of the continuous plane would need a probability density over the whole space instead, and the data give us no such thing beyond the points themselves. The dataset is the natural, practical set of candidates: it is finite, it is already in memory, and updating all the \(D(x_i)\) after each new seed takes one pass over it — \(O(nk)\) distance calculations for all \(k\) seeds.

3. Following the data

Clusters form where the data are dense, so the best first guesses for cluster centres are places where observations actually exist, not arbitrary coordinates. Note how the two ideas combine: an individual point is chosen with probability proportional to \(D(x_i)\), so far-away points are favoured, but a dense group far from the current seeds contains many candidates, and their probabilities add up. That is why k-means++ tends to place one seed in each well-populated region rather than chasing a single isolated point (block 9 looks at when this does and does not protect against outliers).

Precise wording: spread out, not as far apart as possible

It is tempting to say that k-means++ places the seeds "as far apart as possible". That describes the deterministic farthest-first rule, which always takes the single farthest point. k-means++ only makes far points more likely, in proportion to \(D(x_i)\). The randomness is deliberate: it is what lets a dense, distant group outweigh a lone outlier, and it is what gives k-means++ its \(O(\log k)\) guarantee.

The crucial pivot: seeds are only the starting point

k-means++ is purely an initialisation strategy. The data points are used only as the seeds at \(t=0\). The moment the algorithm enters the main loop and computes the first round of means, each centroid becomes the average of its cluster — a floating point in space that is, in general, no longer any data point:

$$\underbrace{\mu_j^{0}\in\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}}_{\text{seeds: data points}} \;\xrightarrow{\text{assign, average}}\; \underbrace{\mu_j^{1}=\frac{1}{|C_j|}\sum_{x_i\in C_j}x_i}_{\text{a mean: anywhere in }\mathbb{R}^d} \;\to\;\cdots$$

From then on, k-means++ and plain random initialisation run the identical Lloyd's algorithm; the only difference is where they started. (A centroid stays exactly on a data point only if its cluster happens to contain a single point. Contrast this with k-medoids, block 9a, where the centres are required to be data points at every step.)

Option 1 in this block also picks the seeds from the data points. So what does k-means++ add?

Both start from data points, so both avoid empty clusters at the first assignment. The difference is how the points are chosen. Option 1 picks all \(k\) uniformly at random, so two seeds can easily land in the same group and leave another group without a seed — the bad start of run B in block 6. k-means++ picks them one at a time and favours points far from the seeds already chosen, which makes that outcome much less likely.

After the first mean update, can a centroid still be exactly one of the data points?

Only by coincidence or in a special case: if its cluster contains exactly one point, its mean is that point. Otherwise the mean of several points is generally a new location. This is the "pivot": the seeds come from the data, the centroids that follow do not have to.

Option 2: k-means++

k-means++ keeps the randomness but biases it toward points that are far from the centres already chosen, so the starting means tend to spread out.

k-means++ seeding
  1. Choose the first mean \(\mu_1^0\) uniformly at random from \(\{x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n\}\).
  2. For \(i=1\) to \(n\): set \(D(x_i)=\lVert x_i-\mu_1^0\rVert^2\).
  3. For \(t=2\) to \(k\):
    1. Choose the new centroid \(\mu_t^0\) from \(X\), picking \(x_i\) with probability proportional to \(D(x_i)\): $$P(x_i)=\frac{D(x_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}D(x_j)}$$
    2. For \(i=1\) to \(n\): set \(D(x_i)=\min\!\left(D(x_i),\ \lVert x_i-\mu_t^0\rVert^2\right)\).
  4. Return the selected centroids \(\{\mu_1^0,\mu_2^0,\dots,\mu_k^0\}\) and proceed with standard k-means from them.

\(D(x_i)\) is always the squared distance from \(x_i\) to the nearest centre chosen so far. Points already covered by a centre have \(D\approx0\) and are almost never picked again; farther points get higher probabilities. This is often called \(D^2\) sampling.

Why it is worth the extra pass

Arthur and Vassilvitskii (2007) proved that the k-means++ seeds alone — before any Lloyd iterations — already have expected cost within a factor \(8(\ln k+2)\) of the optimum:

$$\mathbb{E}\bigl[F_{\text{k-means++}}\bigr]\;\le\;8(\ln k+2)\,F_{\text{OPT}}$$

Uniform random seeding has no such guarantee. The seeding costs \(O(nkd)\), about one extra Lloyd iteration, and it is the default in most libraries.

Suppose three points have \(D\) values \(1, 4, 15\). What is the chance each is chosen as the next centre?

The total is \(20\), so the probabilities are \(1/20=0.05\), \(4/20=0.2\) and \(15/20=0.75\). The far point is the most likely choice, but not a certain one.

9

The farthest-point heuristic

If spreading the centres out is the goal, why not always pick the farthest point outright? Because "farthest" is exactly where outliers live.

The deterministic alternative — farthest-first traversal — replaces the random draw with \(\mu_t^0=\arg\max_i D(x_i)\). The first mean is still chosen at random, and every later choice is forced by it.

The problem

If the data contain an outlier, the farthest point will very often be that outlier, and the algorithm then spends a centre on it. Consider:

  • a cluster of 1000 points near \((0,0)\), and
  • a single outlier point at \((100,100)\).

If the first centroid lands in the main cluster, the farthest point is the outlier, which becomes the second centroid. If you wanted \(k=3\), one centroid is now spent on a single point, and the next "farthest" point may again not represent a real dense cluster. So deterministic farthest-point selection overemphasises rare, far-away points.

What the randomness in k-means++ buys

k-means++ weighs each point by \(D(x_i)\), but a group of points far away collectively carries much more probability than one isolated point. When several genuine clusters are still uncovered, their combined mass usually outweighs a lone outlier.

k-means++ as a weighted roulette wheel

k-means++ chooses each new seed by weighted random sampling. Every point that is not yet a seed gets a weight \(D(x_i)\) — its squared distance to the nearest seed chosen so far — and the next seed is drawn at random with probability proportional to that weight. Picture a roulette wheel:

  • The slices. Every data point gets its own slice, and the width of point \(x_i\)'s slice is its probability \(P(x_i)=D(x_i)\big/\sum_{j}D(x_j)\). Points that are already seeds have \(D=0\): no slice at all.
  • The outlier's slice. A single, very distant outlier gets one very wide slice, because its own \(D\) is huge.
  • A cluster's slices. A dense group of points moderately far away gets many individually narrower slices, one per point.
  • Adding up the area. The chance that the next seed lands somewhere in a group \(G\) is the total width of all its slices:
$$P(\text{next seed}\in G)=\sum_{x_i\in G}P(x_i)=\frac{\sum_{x_i\in G}D(x_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}D(x_j)}$$

So even when the outlier owns the widest single slice, hundreds of narrower slices from a dense, uncovered cluster can take up far more of the wheel in total. The algorithm still picks one point with one random draw, but the combined probability of the cluster dominates.

"Spinning the wheel" is a single uniform random number. Lay the slices end to end, draw \(u\) uniformly from \(\bigl[0,\ \sum_j D(x_j)\bigr)\), and pick the first point whose running total reaches \(u\):

$$\text{choose the smallest } i \text{ with } \sum_{j\le i} D(x_j)\;\ge\;u.$$

Things to try

  • The seed's own cluster nearly vanishes. With the first seed in cluster A, A's points are all close to it, so their slices are tiny: the wheel steers the next seed away from groups that already have one. What wins is not density alone but uncovered mass: many points that are all far from every seed.
  • Widest slice versus most area. With three clusters, the outlier has the widest single slice, but clusters B and C each take far more of the wheel. Spin a few times, or simulate 1,000 spins, and count where the seeds land.
  • Shrink the clusters. Drag "points per cluster" down to 3. With so little mass left in B and C, the outlier's slice becomes a serious contender.
  • One cluster and an outlier (the example from block 9). After the first seed lands in the cluster, there is nothing uncovered except the outlier, so it takes most of the wheel and k-means++ will very probably choose it.
  • Change the slice rule. "Equal" is Option 1, a uniform random pick: the outlier is almost never chosen, but neither is anything steered away from the existing seed, so two seeds often land in the same cluster. "D: plain distance" sits in between. Squaring is what makes far, uncovered regions stand out.
Important difference: squared distance, not distance

It is common to say that each point's probability is "proportional to its distance". In k-means++ it is proportional to the squared distance \(D(x_i)=\min_{s}\lVert x_i-s\rVert^2\) to the nearest seed — hence its other name, \(D^2\) sampling. The square matches the squared distances in the k-means objective, and it is needed for the \(O(\log k)\) guarantee of block 8. Switch the slice rule to "D: plain distance" to see the difference.

An outlier has \(D=100\). Fifty points of an uncovered cluster each have \(D=36\). Everything else has \(D\approx0\). Where will the next seed most likely land?

The cluster's slices add up to \(50\times36=1800\), against \(100\) for the outlier, out of a total of about \(1900\). So the cluster gets about \(1800/1900\approx95\%\) of the wheel and the outlier about \(5\%\), even though the outlier's single slice is almost three times as wide as any one cluster point's.

With the same numbers but plain distance instead of squared distance, how does the outlier's chance change?

The weights become \(\sqrt{100}=10\) for the outlier and \(\sqrt{36}=6\) per cluster point, so \(50\times6=300\) against \(10\): the outlier's share falls to about \(10/310\approx3\%\). Squaring stretches large distances more than small ones, so it rewards far points more strongly; that is what pushes the seeds apart.

9a

k-medoids: centres that are real data points

k-means describes each cluster by an average that may not exist in the data and that one far-away point can drag around. k-medoids insists that every centre is an actual data point, and measures fit by plain (unsquared) distance.

The medoid

The medoid of a cluster \(C\) is the member whose total distance to all the other members is smallest:

$$m(C)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y\,\in\, C}\;\sum_{x\in C} d(x,y)$$

Here \(d\) can be any dissimilarity: Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine, edit distance between strings, or an entry in a table of survey differences. Nothing is ever added or averaged, so k-medoids works even where a "mean" has no meaning — the mean of two DNA sequences or two customer records is not defined, but the most central one of them is.

The objective

Choose a set \(M\) of \(k\) data points as medoids, and charge each point its distance to the nearest one:

$$\min_{\substack{M\subseteq X\\ |M|=k}}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\;{\color{#4A1E5C}{\min_{m\in M}}}\;{\color{#B23A6B}{d(x_i,m)}}$$
Nearest medoidEach point is assigned to the closest of the \(k\) chosen points
Plain distanceNot squared, so far points count in proportion to their distance
Centres from the data\(M\) is a subset of the \(n\) points, so there are \(\binom{n}{k}\) possible choices

Compare the k-means objective in block 4: there the centres are free points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) and the distance is squared. Finding the exact optimum is again NP-hard, so in practice k-medoids is solved by local search.

k-medoids is not k-medians

The names are easily confused. k-medians uses the \(L_1\) distance, and its centre is the coordinate-wise median (block 3) — a point that usually is not in the data. k-medoids restricts the centre to be one of the data points and allows any distance. They coincide only in a special case: in one dimension with an odd-sized cluster, the median is itself a data point, so it is also the medoid.

k-meansk-mediansk-medoids
CentreMeanCoordinate-wise medianMedoid (a data point)
Cost per point\(\lVert x-\mu\rVert_2^2\)\(\lVert x-c\rVert_1\)\(d(x,m)\), any dissimilarity
Centre is a data point?Usually notUsually notAlways
Needs coordinates?YesYesNo — a distance matrix is enough
Effect of an outlierPulls the centre stronglySmallSmall
Centre update for a cluster of \(m\) points\(O(md)\)\(O(md)\)\(O(m^2)\) distance look-ups

Algorithm 1: alternate, as in k-means

k-medoids by alternating assignment and update
  1. Initialise \(k\) medoids by choosing \(k\) data points (at random, or with the k-means++ rule of block 8).
  2. Assign every point to its nearest medoid.
  3. Update each cluster's medoid: for every member \(y\) of the cluster, add up \(d(x,y)\) over the cluster's members, and make the member with the smallest total the new medoid.
  4. Repeat steps 2–3 until the medoids stop changing.

The argument of block 6 carries over unchanged: each step can only lower the objective, there are finitely many medoid sets, so the algorithm stops — at a local minimum. A cluster whose total costs tie is usually left with its current medoid, so the run cannot cycle.

Worked example

Eight points in the plane, \(k=2\), Manhattan distance \(d(x,y)=\lvert x_1-y_1\rvert+\lvert x_2-y_2\rvert\). Point \(H\) is an outlier.

Start from a deliberately poor choice: medoids \(A\) and \(B\), which lie in the same group.

Each number is that member's total distance to the rest of its cluster. Bold marks the smallest total in each cluster, which becomes that cluster's medoid for the next round.

Each "total distance" is a row sum of the matrix restricted to the cluster — for example, in round 2, \(B\)'s total in \(\{A,B,C,D\}\) is \(4+0+1+2=7\). The cost column is the objective before that round's update: in round 2, \((4+5+4)+(4+5+9)=31\). Checking all \(\binom{8}{2}=28\) medoid pairs confirms that \(\{B,E\}\) with cost \(23\) is the global optimum here.

Look at the upper cluster \(\{E,F,G,H\}\). Its mean is \((9.25,\ 6.75)\): not one of the points, and pulled more than two units toward the outlier \(H\). Its medoid is \(E=(7,8)\), sitting among the three points that genuinely belong together.

Robustness to outliers

This is the median argument of block 3 in a new setting. With squared distance a point's pull grows with its distance; with plain distance it does not, so a single far point cannot outvote the rest of the cluster. The restriction to data points adds a second safeguard: the centre can never be an empty spot halfway to an outlier.

Algorithm 2: PAM (partitioning around medoids)

Let \(X\) be the set of all data points, \(M\) the set of selected medoids, \(k\) the target number of medoids, and \(d(x,y)\) the distance between two points. Write \(D(x,M)=\min_{m\in M}d(x,m)\) for the distance from \(x\) to its closest medoid in \(M\). The objective is the total distance from every point to its nearest medoid:

$$F(M)=\sum_{x\in X}\min_{m\in M}d(x,m)=\sum_{x\in X}D(x,M)$$
  1. BUILD (greedy initialisation).
    1. Pick the first medoid as the point with the smallest total distance to all other points: $$m_1=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{c\in X}\;\sum_{x\in X}d(x,c)$$ Set \(M=\{m_1\}\).
    2. Repeatedly add the point that reduces the objective the most: $$c^{*}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{c\in X\setminus M}\;\sum_{x\in X}\min\bigl(D(x,M),\,d(x,c)\bigr)$$ Update \(M=M\cup\{c^{*}\}\), and repeat until \(\lvert M\rvert=k\).
  2. SWAP. For every current medoid \(m\in M\) and every non-medoid \(o\notin M\), compute the change in the objective if \(o\) replaced \(m\): $$\Delta(m,o)=F\bigl((M\setminus\{m\})\cup\{o\}\bigr)-F(M)$$
  3. Evaluate and update.
    1. Find the pair with the smallest change: $$(m^{*},o^{*})=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{m\in M,\;o\notin M}\Delta(m,o)$$
    2. If \(\Delta(m^{*},o^{*})\) is negative, make the swap, \(M=(M\setminus\{m^{*}\})\cup\{o^{*}\}\), and return to step 2.
    3. Otherwise stop: no single swap can lower \(F\), so the medoids have stabilised.

Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths of k-medoids
  • Robust to outliers and noise
  • Works with any dissimilarity, even without coordinates
  • Each centre is a real, interpretable example ("the most typical customer")
  • Needs only a distance matrix — the same input as hierarchical clustering
Weaknesses of k-medoids
  • Much slower than k-means: medoid updates are quadratic in cluster size
  • Storing all pairwise distances takes \(O(n^2)\) memory
  • \(k\) must still be chosen in advance
  • Still a local search; results depend on initialisation
In the worked example, the final medoids are \(\{B,E\}\) with cost \(23\). Would PAM accept swapping \(E\) for the outlier \(H\)?

No. With medoids \(\{B,H\}\), the lower cluster still costs \(4+1+2=7\), but \(E,F,G\) must now go to the nearer of \(B\) and \(H\): \(\min(11,11)+\min(10,12)+\min(9,9)=11+10+9=30\). The total is \(37\), so \(\Delta(E,H)=37-23=+14>0\) and the swap is rejected.

In one dimension with \(d(x,y)=\lvert x-y\rvert\), find the medoid and the mean of \(\{1,2,3,4,100\}\).

The totals are \(1{:}\ 105,\ 2{:}\ 102,\ 3{:}\ 101,\ 4{:}\ 102,\ 100{:}\ 390\), so the medoid is \(3\) — the median, since the cluster has an odd number of points. The mean is \(22\), a value nowhere near four of the five points.

Why can k-medoids cluster text documents compared by edit distance, when k-means cannot?

k-means must compute a mean, which needs the data to be vectors that can be added and divided. Strings cannot be averaged, but the edit distance between any two of them can be computed, and the medoid step only ever compares such distances. So k-medoids, like single, complete and average linkage, needs only the matrix of pairwise dissimilarities.

10

Choosing k

The objective cannot choose \(k\) by itself: adding clusters never makes it worse.

The objective being minimised is \(\min_{Z}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lVert x_i-\mu_{Z_i}\rVert_2^2\). Look at the two extremes:

  • \(k=1\). All points end up in one cluster. The clusters are coarse and say nothing about the data — underfitting.
  • \(k=n\). Every point is its own cluster and the objective is exactly \(0\). Nothing has been learned about the structure of the data — overfitting.

In fact, the best achievable objective is non-increasing in \(k\): with one more centre available you can always reproduce the old solution and do no worse. So minimising \(F\) over \(k\) as well would always choose \(k=n\).

Penalising the number of clusters

As with regularisation, which reduced overfitting in supervised models, add a penalty that grows with \(k\):

$$\min_{k,\;Z_1,\dots,Z_n}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\lVert x_i-\mu_{Z_i}\bigr\rVert_2^2\;+\;\lambda\,f(k)$$
ApproachPenalty \(f(k)\)Idea
AIC (Akaike information criterion)\(2kd\)Penalises the number of parameters: each cluster has \(d\) parameters (its centroid coordinates).
BIC (Bayesian information criterion)\(kd\log n\)Stronger penalty for larger datasets; favours simpler models.
MDL (minimum description length)\(\propto k\log n\)Based on information compression; similar to BIC.
Simple linear penalty (heuristic)\(k\)Quick, intuitive penalty directly proportional to the number of clusters.
Units matter

AIC and BIC are defined on a log-likelihood. If the clusters are modelled as spherical Gaussians with a shared variance \(\sigma^2\), the negative log-likelihood is \(F/(2\sigma^2)\) plus a constant, so on the scale of \(F\) the penalty weight is \(\lambda\approx 2\sigma^2\) (up to the conventions of each criterion). In practice \(\sigma^2\) must be estimated, and \(\lambda\) behaves like any other hyperparameter.

Two widely used alternatives (added)

The elbow method

Plot the minimised \(F\) against \(k\). The drop is steep while each new centre splits a genuine group, then flattens once centres start splitting groups that were already well described. Choose \(k\) at the bend. It is quick but subjective: many datasets have no sharp elbow.

The silhouette score

For each point \(i\), let \(a(i)\) be its mean distance to the other members of its own cluster, and \(b(i)\) its mean distance to the members of the nearest other cluster. Then

$$s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),\,b(i)\}}\;\in[-1,1]$$

\(s(i)\) near \(1\) means the point sits well inside its cluster; near \(0\), on a border; negative, probably in the wrong cluster. Averaging \(s(i)\) over all points and choosing the \(k\) with the highest average is a common rule; unlike SSE, the average silhouette does not automatically improve with \(k\).

Why can't \(k\) be chosen by running k-means for each \(k\) and keeping the one with the smallest SSE?

Because the smallest SSE is always at the largest \(k\) tried, and at \(k=n\) it is zero. SSE measures fit, not whether the extra clusters are real. A criterion for \(k\) must reward fit and charge for complexity, as the penalised objective, the elbow and the silhouette each do in their own way.

11

Feature scaling and failure modes (added)

k-means measures everything with Euclidean distance to a single centre. That hides two assumptions worth knowing before trusting its output.

Scale the features first

Euclidean distance adds squared differences across features, so a feature measured in large units dominates. Standardising each feature to zero mean and unit variance, \(x_{\cdot j}\leftarrow (x_{\cdot j}-\bar x_j)/s_j\), gives every feature a comparable say.

What k-means implicitly assumes

Minimising squared distance to one centre works best when clusters are roughly spherical, of similar spread, and convex. Each of the following breaks one of these assumptions.

Some of these cases are handled by other methods. Single-linkage hierarchical clustering (block 14) follows chains of nearby points and separates the two moons; Gaussian mixture models allow stretched and differently sized clusters; density-based methods such as DBSCAN also handle arbitrary shapes and label outliers explicitly.

Strengths of k-means
  • Simple and fast: \(O(nkd)\) per iteration
  • Scales to millions of points
  • Centroids are an interpretable summary of each cluster
  • Assigns new points directly (nearest centroid)
Weaknesses of k-means
  • \(k\) must be chosen in advance
  • Only a local optimum; depends on initialisation
  • Assumes convex, similarly sized, roughly spherical clusters
  • Sensitive to feature scaling and to outliers
Part C
Hierarchical clustering
12

Hierarchies and dendrograms

Hierarchical clustering also groups similar data, but instead of one partition it builds a whole family of nested partitions, arranged as a tree.

k-means requires the number of clusters \(k\) before it starts. Hierarchical clustering does not: it records every level of grouping, from \(n\) singletons to one cluster, and \(k\) is chosen afterwards by deciding where to cut the tree.

Two directions

  • Agglomerative (bottom-up). Start with each point as its own cluster and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until all points belong to one cluster. This is by far the more common variant, and the one worked through below.
  • Divisive (top-down). Start with all points in one cluster and repeatedly split a cluster into smaller ones until each point is in its own cluster. Choosing the best split exactly is expensive, so divisive methods use a heuristic split — for example running 2-means on the cluster (bisecting k-means).

Reading a dendrogram

The tree is drawn as a dendrogram:

  • It is a tree diagram showing how clusters are merged (or split).
  • The height at which two clusters are joined represents their distance, or dissimilarity.
  • Cutting the dendrogram at a chosen height decides the number of clusters: the branches that cross the cut are the clusters.
In the A–I dendrogram, which pair of leaves is the most similar, and how many clusters does a cut between merges 5 and 6 produce?

\(A\) and \(B\), joined first at the lowest height. A cut above merge 5 but below merge 6 leaves four clusters: \(\{A,B,C,D\}\), \(\{E\}\), \(\{F,G\}\), \(\{H,I\}\).

Watching both directions build the tree

The explorer runs either method on the same points. In agglomerative mode it merges the two closest clusters under the chosen linkage, from the bottom of the tree upwards. In divisive mode it uses bisecting k-means: at each step it takes the cluster with the largest within-cluster sum of squares (SSE) and splits it in two with 2-means, from the top of the tree downwards. Solid branches have already been built; dashed branches are the merges or splits still to come.

The pink line is the cut. Step through the run, drag the slider, or drag the line up and down on the dendrogram: the clusters it creates are shown on the scatter plot and listed below, together with the count formula.

How many clusters does a cut create?

Number the merges \(1,2,\dots,n-1\) in the order they happen, with heights \(h_1\le h_2\le\dots\le h_{n-1}\) (monotone linkages, block 18). A cut made after the \(i\)-th merge, that is at any height \(h\) with \(h_i\le h\lt h_{i+1}\), crosses

$$c(i)=n-i\qquad i=0,1,\dots,n-1,\qquad\text{taking } h_0=0,\; h_n=\infty$$

branches. Each merge replaces two clusters by one, so every merge lowers the count by exactly one: \(n\) singletons before any merge, one cluster after all \(n-1\).

Read top-down, a divisive tree is the mirror image. After the \(j\)-th split there are

$$c(j)=j+1\qquad j=0,1,\dots,n-1.$$

For the same tree, a cut that leaves \(c\) clusters lies after \(i=n-c\) merges counted from the bottom, or after \(j=c-1\) splits counted from the top, so

$$i+j=n-1.$$

So to get \(k\) clusters, stop the agglomerative run after \(n-k\) merges, or the divisive run after \(k-1\) splits.

Two details

Ties. If two merges happen at exactly the same height, a horizontal cut cannot fall between them, and some counts \(n-i\) are skipped. The formula still holds when the cut is described by "after the \(i\)-th merge".

The two directions do not give the same tree. Switch between them on the 12-point data: bisecting k-means first splits all 12 points 6 / 6, cutting one natural group in half, while agglomerative clustering keeps the three groups intact until the very end. Greedy merging and greedy splitting each commit to their early decisions, from opposite ends.

With \(n=12\) points, after how many merges, or after how many splits, does a cut give 3 clusters?

Agglomerative: \(n-i=3\), so \(i=9\) merges. Divisive: \(j+1=3\), so \(j=2\) splits. And \(9+2=11=n-1\).

In single linkage on the lecture's six points, where can a cut give exactly 4 clusters?

Four clusters means \(i=n-4=2\) merges, so the cut must lie between \(h_2=1.414\) and \(h_3=1.803\). It crosses the branches \(\{P_0\}\), \(\{P_1,P_2\}\), \(\{P_3,P_4\}\) and \(\{P_5\}\).

13

The proximity matrix and the agglomerative loop

Every agglomerative method is the same loop over a matrix of distances. Only one line — how the distance between two clusters is defined — changes.

After choosing a distance measure between points, compute the pairwise distances of all points and store them in the proximity matrix \(D\). The running example uses six points and Euclidean distance.

P0P1P2P3P4P5
P003.04144.12312.82844.24264.1231
P13.041401.11801.80282.50004.0311
P24.12311.118002.23612.23614.2426
P32.82841.80282.236101.41422.2361
P44.24262.50002.23611.414202.2361
P54.12314.03114.24262.23612.23610

Proximity matrix. It is symmetric with zeros on the diagonal, so only the upper triangle (dark figures) is needed. The smallest entry, \(d(P_1,P_2)=\sqrt{0.5^2+1^2}\approx1.118\), is marked.

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering
  1. Start. Treat each data point as its own cluster, so initially there are \(n\) clusters.
  2. Compute the distance matrix. Compute \(d(x_i,x_j)\) for every pair and store it in \(D\).
  3. Find the closest clusters. Identify the two clusters \(A,B\) with the smallest distance \(D(A,B)\) under the chosen linkage.
  4. Merge \(A\) and \(B\) into a single new cluster.
  5. Update the distance matrix. Remove the rows and columns for \(A\) and \(B\); add a row and column for the new cluster, with its distance to every other cluster \(C\) computed from the linkage.
  6. Repeat steps 3–5 until one cluster remains (or until the desired number of clusters \(k\) is reached).
  7. Construct the dendrogram from the sequence of merges and the distances at which they happened.

New clusters are numbered after the original points: the first merge creates \(P_6\), the next \(P_7\), and so on up to \(P_{10}\), which contains all six points.

The four linkages

LinkageCluster distance \(D(A,B)\)Update for merged cluster \(A\cup B\)
Single (minimum)\(\displaystyle\min_{x_i\in A,\,x_j\in B} d(x_i,x_j)\)\(\min\bigl(D(A,C),D(B,C)\bigr)\)
Complete (maximum)\(\displaystyle\max_{x_i\in A,\,x_j\in B} d(x_i,x_j)\)\(\max\bigl(D(A,C),D(B,C)\bigr)\)
Average (UPGMA)\(\displaystyle\frac{1}{|A||B|}\sum_{x_i\in A}\sum_{x_j\in B} d(x_i,x_j)\)\(\dfrac{|A|\,D(A,C)+|B|\,D(B,C)}{|A|+|B|}\)
Centroid\(d(\mu_A,\mu_B)\)\(\mu_{\text{new}}=\dfrac{|A|\mu_A+|B|\mu_B}{|A|+|B|}\), then \(d(\mu_{\text{new}},\mu_C)\)
One formula for all of them: Lance–Williams

Each update above is a special case of

$$D(A\cup B,\,C)=\alpha_A D(A,C)+\alpha_B D(B,C)+\beta\,D(A,B)+\gamma\,\bigl|D(A,C)-D(B,C)\bigr|$$
  • Single linkage: \(\alpha_A=\alpha_B=\tfrac12,\ \beta=0,\ \gamma=-\tfrac12\), which gives \(\tfrac12(a+b)-\tfrac12|a-b|=\min(a,b)\).
  • Complete linkage: the same with \(\gamma=+\tfrac12\), giving the maximum.
  • Average linkage: \(\alpha_A=\tfrac{|A|}{|A|+|B|},\ \alpha_B=\tfrac{|B|}{|A|+|B|},\ \beta=\gamma=0\). This is why the update never has to revisit the original points.
  • Centroid linkage: \(\alpha_A=\frac{|A|}{|A|+|B|},\ \alpha_B=\frac{|B|}{|A|+|B|},\ \beta=-\frac{|A|\,|B|}{(|A|+|B|)^2},\ \gamma=0\), valid only when \(D\) is the squared Euclidean distance between centroids. The negative \(\beta\) corrects for the merged centroid lying between \(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_B\). Check with the lecture's points: merging \(P_1,P_2\) into \(P_6\) gives \(D(P_6,P_0)=\tfrac12\cdot 9.25+\tfrac12\cdot 17-\tfrac14\cdot 1.25=12.8125\) (squares of \(3.0414\), \(4.1231\) and \(1.118\)), and \(\sqrt{12.8125}=3.5795\), the value in block 17. The lecture's matrices store plain distances, so square them before the update and take the square root after; plugging in plain distances gives \(3.303\), which is wrong.
  • Because \(\beta\) is negative for centroid linkage, the new distance can be smaller than both \(D(A,C)\) and \(D(B,C)\). That is exactly the inversion of block 18: there \(D(P_5,P_2)=\tfrac23\cdot 12.25+\tfrac13\cdot 13-\tfrac29\cdot 11.25=10\), so the merge happens at \(\sqrt{10}=3.162\), below the previous merge at \(3.354\).
What do the time and memory of this naive loop grow like?

The matrix has \(O(n^2)\) entries, so memory is \(O(n^2)\). There are \(n-1\) merges; scanning the matrix for its minimum each time costs \(O(n^2)\), so the naive loop is \(O(n^3)\). Keeping each row's candidates in a priority queue brings this to \(O(n^2\log n)\), and single linkage has an \(O(n^2)\) algorithm (SLINK). Either way, hierarchical clustering is practical for thousands of points, not millions — compare k-means' \(O(nkd)\) per iteration.

14

Single (minimum) linkage

Two clusters are as close as their closest pair of points.

$$D(A,B)=\min_{x_i\in A,\;x_j\in B} d(x_i,x_j)\qquad\qquad D(\text{new},C)=\min\bigl(D(A,C),\,D(B,C)\bigr)$$

In words: identify the two clusters with the smallest distance between them, where that distance is the shortest distance between any two points across the clusters. After merging, the new cluster's distance to any other cluster \(C\) is simply the smaller of the two old distances.

Start from the proximity matrix of block 13. Its smallest entry is \(d(P_1,P_2)=1.1180\), so \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) merge first.

Complete (maximum) linkage

Two clusters are as close as their farthest pair of points. Complete linkage merges the pair with the smallest maximum inter-cluster distance.

$$D(A,B)=\max_{x_i\in A,\;x_j\in B} d(x_i,x_j)\qquad\qquad D(\text{new},C)=\max\bigl(D(A,C),\,D(B,C)\bigr)$$

The steps are those of block 13 with this definition. Because a merge is only cheap when every pair of points is close, complete linkage favours compact clusters of similar diameter.

Start from the proximity matrix of block 13. Its smallest entry is \(d(P_1,P_2)=1.1180\), so \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) merge first.

16

Average linkage

Two clusters are as close as the average of all cross-cluster pairs — a compromise between the two extremes.

$$D(A,B)=\frac{1}{|A|\,|B|}\sum_{x_i\in A}\sum_{x_j\in B} d(x_i,x_j) \qquad\qquad D(\text{new},C)=\frac{|A|\cdot D(A,C)+|B|\cdot D(B,C)}{|A|+|B|}$$

The update is a size-weighted average, so a cluster of four points counts four times as much as a single point. It gives exactly the same result as recomputing the average over all pairs from scratch.

Why the size-weighted update is exact

By definition, the distance between any two clusters \(X\) and \(Y\) is the average of all pairwise distances between their points:

$$D(X,Y)=\frac{1}{\lvert X\rvert\,\lvert Y\rvert}\sum_{x\in X}\sum_{y\in Y}d(x,y)$$

Step 1: set up the distance for the merged cluster. We want the distance between the newly merged cluster \(A\cup B\) and a third cluster \(C\). Applying the definition:

$$D(A\cup B,\,C)=\frac{1}{\lvert A\cup B\rvert\cdot\lvert C\rvert}\sum_{x\in A\cup B}\;\sum_{y\in C}d(x,y)$$

Step 2: expand the terms. The clusters \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, so the merged cluster has \(\lvert A\cup B\rvert=\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert\) points, and a sum over the points of \(A\cup B\) is the sum over \(A\) plus the sum over \(B\):

$$D(A\cup B,\,C)=\frac{1}{\bigl(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert\bigr)\lvert C\rvert}\left(\sum_{x\in A}\sum_{y\in C}d(x,y)+\sum_{x\in B}\sum_{y\in C}d(x,y)\right)$$

Step 3: relate the sums to the old cluster distances. The distances from \(A\) and from \(B\) to \(C\) were computed with the same definition:

$$D(A,C)=\frac{1}{\lvert A\rvert\,\lvert C\rvert}\sum_{x\in A}\sum_{y\in C}d(x,y),\qquad D(B,C)=\frac{1}{\lvert B\rvert\,\lvert C\rvert}\sum_{x\in B}\sum_{y\in C}d(x,y)$$

Rearranging each one isolates its double sum:

$$\sum_{x\in A}\sum_{y\in C}d(x,y)=\lvert A\rvert\,\lvert C\rvert\cdot D(A,C),\qquad \sum_{x\in B}\sum_{y\in C}d(x,y)=\lvert B\rvert\,\lvert C\rvert\cdot D(B,C)$$

Step 4: substitute and simplify. Putting these into the expanded expression from Step 2:

$$D(A\cup B,\,C)=\frac{1}{\bigl(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert\bigr)\lvert C\rvert}\Bigl(\lvert A\rvert\,\lvert C\rvert\cdot D(A,C)+\lvert B\rvert\,\lvert C\rvert\cdot D(B,C)\Bigr)$$

Factor \(\lvert C\rvert\) out of the bracket:

$$D(A\cup B,\,C)=\frac{\lvert C\rvert\,\Bigl(\lvert A\rvert\cdot D(A,C)+\lvert B\rvert\cdot D(B,C)\Bigr)}{\bigl(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert\bigr)\lvert C\rvert}$$

and cancel \(\lvert C\rvert\) from the numerator and the denominator. What remains is exactly the size-weighted update:

$$D(A\cup B,\,C)=\frac{\lvert A\rvert\cdot D(A,C)+\lvert B\rvert\cdot D(B,C)}{\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert}$$

Nothing has been approximated: the update gives the same value as averaging all \(\bigl(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert\bigr)\lvert C\rvert\) pairwise distances again, but it needs only two numbers from the old matrix and the two cluster sizes. Note that \(\lvert C\rvert\) cancels, so the size of the third cluster never enters the update.

18

Monotonicity and centroid inversions

A dendrogram is only readable if later merges sit higher than earlier ones. Centroid linkage can break that rule.

Monotonicity

  • In standard, well-behaved hierarchical clustering, the distance between the clusters being merged is non-decreasing as the hierarchy is built up: if merge \(s\) happens at height \(h_s\), then \(h_1\le h_2\le\dots\le h_{n-1}\).
  • This keeps the dendrogram consistent: every new fusion sits at least as high as the one before, so a horizontal cut at any height gives a well-defined partition.

Single, complete, average and Ward linkage are all guaranteed to be monotone. Centroid linkage (and its cousin, median linkage) is not.

The problem with centroids

When two clusters merge, the new centroid lies somewhere between the old ones. It can end up closer to a third cluster than either original cluster was, so the next merge happens at a smaller distance than the last. This is an inversion.

A four-point example: \(P_0=(0,0),\ P_1=(0,1),\ P_2=(0,4),\ P_3=(3,2)\).

Candidate mergeCentroidsDistance
After merge 1 (\(P_4=\{P_0,P_1\}\), centroid \((0,0.5)\))
\(P_3\) with \(P_4\)\((3,2)\) and \((0,0.5)\)3.3541 ← smallest
\(P_2\) with \(P_4\)\((0,4)\) and \((0,0.5)\)3.5000
\(P_2\) with \(P_3\)\((0,4)\) and \((3,2)\)3.6056
After merge 2 (\(P_5=\{P_0,P_1,P_3\}\), centroid \((1,1)\))
\(P_2\) with \(P_5\)\((0,4)\) and \((1,1)\)3.1623 < 3.3541

Merging \(P_3\) pulled the centroid from \((0,0.5)\) to \((1,1)\) — toward \(P_2\)'s side of the plane. So the final merge happens at \(3.162\), below the previous merge at \(3.354\).

Did the six-point centroid walkthrough in block 17 have an inversion?

No. Its merge distances were \(1.118,\ 1.414,\ 2.016,\ 3.105,\ 3.342\) — strictly increasing. Centroid linkage can invert, but does not have to; inversions appear when a merge moves a centroid noticeably toward a third cluster.

Chaining versus compactness

Single linkage only needs one close pair to merge two clusters, so a thin trail of points can link two otherwise separate groups — the chaining effect. Complete linkage needs every pair to be close, so it produces compact clusters but can split a large, elongated one. Average linkage sits in between.

Chaining is a weakness here, but the same property is a strength when clusters really are long and curved:

Ward's linkage

Ward's method is the linkage most closely tied to k-means. It merges the pair of clusters whose union causes the smallest increase in the k-means objective (total within-cluster sum of squares):

$$\Delta(A,B)=\sum_{x\in A\cup B}\lVert x-\mu_{A\cup B}\rVert^2-\sum_{x\in A}\lVert x-\mu_A\rVert^2-\sum_{x\in B}\lVert x-\mu_B\rVert^2=\frac{|A|\,|B|}{|A|+|B|}\,\lVert\mu_A-\mu_B\rVert^2$$

It is like centroid linkage, but the factor \(\tfrac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|}\) makes it expensive to merge two large clusters, and unlike centroid linkage it is monotone. On the six points it merges in the same order as complete linkage. (Libraries often report the height as \(\sqrt{2\Delta}\), which equals the plain Euclidean distance for two single points — hence the first Ward merge also appears at \(1.118\).) Ward's tree is a popular way to pick \(k\) and initial centroids for k-means.

LinkageTends to produceMonotoneWatch out for
SingleLong, chained, arbitrarily shaped clustersYesChaining through noise and bridges
CompleteCompact clusters of similar diameterYesSensitive to outliers; splits large elongated clusters
AverageA balance of the twoYesLess intuitive to reason about
CentroidClusters summarised by their meansNoInversions in the dendrogram
WardCompact, similarly sized, roughly spherical clustersYesSame shape assumptions as k-means
For two single points \(a\) and \(b\), what is Ward's merge cost?

\(|A|=|B|=1\), so \(\Delta=\tfrac{1\cdot1}{2}\lVert a-b\rVert^2=\tfrac12\lVert a-b\rVert^2\). Check: the merged centroid is the midpoint, and each point is \(\tfrac12\lVert a-b\rVert\) from it, giving \(2\cdot\tfrac14\lVert a-b\rVert^2\). The reported height \(\sqrt{2\Delta}=\lVert a-b\rVert\) is just the distance.

Testing the claims yourself

The table above and the usual "comparison of linkage methods" figure make claims such as "single linkage chains through noise" or "Ward handles noise best". The explorer below lets you check them. It runs all five linkages on the same data, cuts each tree into \(k\) clusters, and shows:

  • The clusters, coloured to match the true groups as closely as possible. Noise points and outliers have a dark outline.
  • The adjusted Rand index (ARI) against the true groups, ignoring noise points: \(1\) means a perfect match, \(0\) means no better than chance.
  • The cluster sizes, which expose a common failure: one giant cluster plus a few single points.
  • What decided the last merge before the cut: the closest pair for single linkage, the farthest pair for complete, the average distance for average, and the two centroids for Ward and centroid linkage.
  • The top of each dendrogram (the last 13 merges; the numbers under the leaves are cluster sizes) with the cut in pink, and whether the tree has any inversions.

What the explorer shows about each claim

ClaimTryWhat you see
Single linkage handles non-globular shapesNested circles, Two moons (no noise)True: single is the only method with ARI 1; the others cut the shapes in half.
Single linkage chains through noise and bridgesAny dataset with 5% noise; Two blobs and a bridgeTrue: one giant cluster plus single points. The last-merge line shows the tiny gap it jumped.
Average and complete work well on globular data, with mixed results otherwiseSeparated blobs, then Two moons and Stretched clustersTrue: perfect on blobs, mediocre on moons, poor on stretched clusters.
Complete linkage splits large, elongated clustersStretched clustersTrue: it has the lowest ARI there, cutting across the long shapes.
Complete linkage is sensitive to outliersBlobs with outliersNot in this test: complete and Ward keep the three groups, while single, average and centroid waste clusters on outliers. See the note below.
Ward is the most effective for noisy dataDifferent densities with 10% noiseTrue for noisy globular data: Ward keeps its high ARI while average collapses. On non-globular shapes (circles, moons) Ward fails like the others.
Only centroid linkage is non-monotoneAny datasetTrue: centroid linkage shows several inversions on every dataset; the others never do.
Correction: complete linkage and outliers

"Sensitive to outliers" is often said of complete linkage because a single far point sets the diameter of whatever cluster it joins: the cluster then looks larger than it is, and later merges are decided by that one point. That effect is real, but it does not mean complete linkage is the worst choice when outliers are present. Single and average linkage leave isolated points unmerged until the very end, so with a fixed \(k\) they often spend whole clusters on individual outliers, as the explorer shows. Treat the table entry as "the outlier distorts merge heights", not "complete linkage loses the groups".

On the nested circles, why does single linkage succeed while Ward fails, even though Ward is "best on noisy data"?

Ward merges the pair that increases the within-cluster sum of squares the least, which favours compact, roughly round clusters — the same assumption as k-means. A ring is not compact: its centre is empty, so Ward prefers to cut each ring into halves. Single linkage only needs a chain of close neighbours, which a ring provides. "Best on noisy data" is a statement about globular groups.

Why does adding just 5% of random points ruin single linkage on the two moons?

Single linkage merges two clusters as soon as any pair of their points is close. A few random points in the gap between the moons create a chain of short steps from one moon to the other, so the moons merge long before the noise points themselves are absorbed. The last-merge line in the Single panel shows the short step it took.

You have 2 million customer records and want 8 segments. Which method, and why?

k-means (with k-means++ and a few restarts, after standardising features). A hierarchical method would need a distance matrix with about \(2\times10^{12}\) entries, which is far beyond memory, while k-means costs \(O(nkd)\) per iteration. If the number of segments were unknown, a common compromise is to run hierarchical clustering on a random sample or on a few hundred k-means centroids and read \(k\) off that dendrogram.

A biologist has 60 gene-expression profiles and wants to see how they group at several levels of detail. Which method?

Hierarchical clustering. With \(n=60\) the \(O(n^2)\) cost is trivial, the number of groups is not known in advance, and the dendrogram shows the nested structure directly — which groups are near-duplicates and which only join at the top. Average or complete linkage with a correlation-based dissimilarity is a typical choice for expression data.
